doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Cannonball Adderley and why he refused Miles Davis
summary: He calls Cannonball corny but skilled, and turned down gigs with Miles over unreliable pay.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: How about Cannonball Adderley? Did you become aware...

Cannonball didn’t even come to New York until after Charlie Parker was dead. So he was a big thing. But he’d have come while Charlie Parker was alive, he wouldn’t have been anything like that. But he could play. He was nice. He was a nice guy as far as I know. He played a little Country-and-Western. Sometimes he sounded like a hillbilly, but...
I mean, he played corny. You know what “corny” is, don’t you?

All right. He played corny. But he knew the saxophone. He knew it. In fact, Miles asked me to play with him two or three times when he had Coltrane there, but I wouldn’t play with Miles, because Miles wasn’t reliable with money, and I couldn’t afford to play a week without bringing in some kind of income.

No. No way. Because I didn’t want to do what you have to do to people like that. Because he was an icon, people liked him, and I wouldn’t want nobody to see me hit him upside the head with a baseball bat or something.
Were you a fan of his music?
Yeah. I was a fan of his musicians. Red Garland I loved. Paul Chambers. And Philly.
